newsitem.title: USA: Albright cites chemical pact as priority.
newsitem.headline: Albright cites chemical pact as priority.

text.p: Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright said on Wednesday her earliest priority was winning Senate ratification of the international chemical weapons treaty and the administration would have a "robust battle plan" to achieve that goal.

But victory remains an uphill battle. Key Senate Republicans -- including Majority Leader Trent Lott and Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms -- have opposed the pact and shown no public sign of softening.

If the United States does not ratify the pact by April 29, it will not be a founding signatory of the pact and hence lose out on placing upwards of two dozen Americans in the organisation that will make rules to implement the treaty.

Negotiations on the Chemical Weapons Convention were completed under former President George Bush and more than 180 countries have signed it. It bans the production, stockpiling and use of chemical arms.

But critics like Helms say it cannot be verified and puts an unwarranted burden on firms that use chemicals for purposes unrelated to weapons, such as fertlizer production. Much of the U.S. chemical industry supports the treaty, however.

The Chemical Weapons Convention "is no panacea but it will make it more difficult for rogue states and others hostile to our interests to develop or obtain chemical weapons," Albright said at her Senate Foreign Relations Committee confirmation hearing to be the first woman U.S. Secretary of State.
She appealed for cooperation to get the pact through the Senate, which planned to take up the issue last year but put it aside when it became embroiled in elections.
Republican Sen. Richard Lugar of Indiana, an influential voice on national security issues, pressed Albright and the administration to address the matter urgently.
He said he was gravely concerned there could be a chemical attack by a terrorist group in the United States like that which occurred in the Tokyo subway two years ago.
The treaty is "in our absolute vital security interest" and if Washington does not ratify the pact it could lead to the dissolution of other arms control treaties, Lugar said.
Albright said she shared Lugar's concern that a chemical attack could happen in the United States and believed it essential that Washington became an original party.
"We will be having a robust battle plan to work with you and other members of the Senate so that we can, in fact, get this convention ratified," she promised, without providing details.
